profiles.summary: No new opcode or precompile difference was found. A sweep of 4,432 low and patterned addresses on the official node returned the same special set as cycle 2. Both public replay clients carry a list of early mainnet transactions where the validator node handled SELFDESTRUCT differently from revm. That is the one execution divergence the clients record, and core does not use that opcode.

deltas.delta: Empty calldata calls to every address from 0x0000 to 0x10ff, 0x2000 to 0x200f, 0x3000 to 0x300f, 0x4200 to 0x420f, 0x5000 to 0x500f and 0xfff0 to 0xffff answered like accounts without code, except 0x02, 0x03, 0x06 to 0x0a and 0x0800 to 0x0814. 0x0809 returned the L1 block number and the other twenty read precompiles returned PrecompileError. deltas.delta: The official replay client removes the state change of one address after each of 18 mainnet transactions in blocks 1,467,569 to 1,531,366 and labels them improper self destructs (run.rs lines 61 to 92). The archive client carries the same 18 entries (patch.rs lines 7 to 26). The validator node therefore did not follow revm's SELFDESTRUCT handling in those early blocks. No later block is listed. I could not read the commit that explains the cause, because github.com is blocked in this session.

The archive client still maps both of its spec ids to revm's CANCUN and replaces only BLOCKHASH below block 243,538 (spec.rs lines 14 to 19, api/mod.rs lines 33 to 43). Rechecked on 2026-11-23, unchanged since cycle 2.

The HyperEVM page states that transactions without EIP-155 replay protection are accepted. A transaction signed for another chain without a chain id can be replayed here. This acts on the account that signed it and needs the same target address on both chains. The HyperEVM PoolManager address 0x12D4Fd9C5DeDd00ab8a0bCe2CF0167bbf94b6B1F is used on no other of the 21 networks.

profiles.summary: The open point behind F-020 is settled by chain data: the first transaction ever sent from the USDC treasury address is an unsigned system transaction, and the address has never acted on HyperCore. In 4,725 sampled blocks all 1,927 system transactions sat ahead of the signed ones, and a HYPE credit debits the bridge address by exactly the amount credited. The validator node is closed source, so the clearance of assumption A1 still rests on the two replay clients.

deltas.delta: The archive client's check of the receipts root leaves out receipts whose cumulative gas is zero, which are the system transactions (reth_copy.rs lines 41 to 47). Its header check therefore covers the outcome of signed transactions only. The official replay client compares the receipt of a system transaction with the recorded one when the block data carries it (run.rs lines 217 to 238). An indexer vendor reports that the transactions root and receipts root of HyperEVM headers match the block without its system transactions.

The docs state that the HyperEVM mempool is on-chain state, accepts only the next 8 nonces of each address and prunes transactions older than one day. These rules act on the sender's own account. I found no way for another account to use them against a liquidity provider.

profiles.summary: No special address answers the PoolManager differently when the PoolManager is an inner frame with another transaction origin. The Elysium bridge contract on HyperEVM sends HYPE to the HyperCore bridge address and calls CoreWriter when a child chain message tells it to, and both acts reach only the bridge contract's own HyperCore account. The hooks that serve most pools refuse or ignore pools they did not register.

findings.title: HyperCore moves USDC out of the AQAv2 treasury address with unsigned transactions although that address has never signed anything, so a validator vote that named the PoolManager would need no act by it
findings.difference: HyperCore injects system transactions into HyperEVM blocks. They carry no signature, pay no gas and the node sets the sender. Under AQAv2 the node sends such transactions in the name of two addresses, the linked contract of the quote token and a treasury address that the treasury deployer designates, to hold their token balances in a 1 to 9 ratio. Activation is by validator vote. On Ethereum a balance leaves an address only through a transaction that the address signed or a call that its own code made.
findings.mechanism: 1. Earlier cycles could not tell whether the designated treasury address has to agree on chain. The chain answers this. The USDC treasury address 0xc20699185c15D0a2fD65779BB5d69f5b0B113c00 had nonce 0 and 0 HYPE at block 37,597,802, so it had never sent an EVM transaction and could not have paid for one. Its first transaction, in block 37,597,803 on 2026-06-12, is a system transaction with nonce 0, gas price 0 and no signature that calls transfer on USDC and moves 2,001 USDC to the CoreDepositWallet. The HyperCore info API reports that the address does not exist as a HyperCore user and has never sent a HyperCore action. The authorizeAqav2Role action has the fields token and role only, and the staking account that sent it for Coinbase is a different address. No on-chain act by the treasury address preceded the transfers. Coinbase named both addresses in public, which is consent outside the protocol. 2. The node also sends USDC transfers in the name of the CoreDepositWallet, which is a contract. A system transaction can therefore carry a contract address as sender. 3. If a validator vote activated AQAv2 for a token with the PoolManager as treasury address, the node would send transfer calls on that token with the PoolManager as msg.sender whenever the 9 to 1 rule calls for a transfer toward the linked contract. The token treats them as transfers by the holder. 4. Nothing in src sees this. Pool accounting is never compared with a token balance. sync reads the balance only to open a measuring window (src/PoolManager.sol:279-288) and settle credits only a rise inside that window (src/PoolManager.sol:349-365). The currency's pools and claims would still record the tokens as owed, and the last takes of that currency would revert in the token transfer (src/types/Currency.sol:55-87). 5. What I could not find out: whether HyperCore checks the designated address in any way, for example refuses an address with code, whether the treasury deployer can change the address after activation, and the exact rebalancing rule. No public source states them and the validator node is closed source.
findings.impact: All pools and ERC-6909 claims in a quote token whose AQAv2 treasury address were set to the PoolManager. USDC is the only AQAv2 token today, its treasury address is Coinbase's, and the PoolManager holds 997.75 USDC. An ordinary account cannot bring this about.
findings.preconditions: A treasury deployer and a technical deployer that each stake 500,000 HYPE, and a validator vote that activates AQAv2 with the PoolManager as treasury address or changes an existing designation to it. The balance of the token's linked contract must sit below its 10 percent share for transfers to flow out of the treasury address.
findings.mitigations: Ask the Hyperliquid team whether a treasury designation is checked against the named address and whether it can change after activation. Watch eth_getSystemTxsByBlockNumber for a system transaction whose sender is the PoolManager. Liquidity providers in AQAv2 quote tokens depend on the validator set for this in the same way as for any other system transaction.

findings.title: Measured on the deployed contract, one empty bitmap word costs about 5,900 gas in the swap loop, so a small block fits about 500 words and a big block cannot hold a walk across the whole range at tick spacing 1
findings.difference: HyperEVM small blocks hold 3,000,000 gas and big blocks 30,000,000 gas, and a sender reaches big blocks only after a HyperCore action sets a flag on its account. In 4,725 sampled blocks 78 were big blocks. F-039 derived the cost of the swap loop from repository snapshots and gave about 1,283 empty words per small block. This entry replaces those estimates with measurements on the deployed PoolManager.
findings.mechanism: Pool.swap runs one loop iteration per bitmap word or initialized tick on its way (src/libraries/Pool.sol:344-437, src/libraries/TickBitmap.sol:85-121). I called the deployed Quoter for 63 swaps of 2^100 input units in hookless pools at block 51,997,409 on an archive node, took the gas of the PoolManager.swap frame from callTracer and counted the bitmap slots and tick slots the frame read with prestateTracer. The 49 swaps without a tick crossing read 11 to 63 words and fit a line of 5,871 gas per word plus 39,059 gas. Two pools with tick spacing 10 read 179 words and used 1,080,157 and 1,080,189 gas, which is 5,816 gas per word. One tick crossing added 10,917 to 31,243 gas and two crossings added 61,692 gas (Pool.sol:413-428 and 602-612). The floor of 2,242 gas per iteration in F-039 counted the bitmap read only. The measured figure includes the price computation and the swap step of each iteration. With these figures a 3,000,000 gas transaction holds at most about 504 empty words or about 95 to 270 crossings. At tick spacing 1 the walk from tick 0 to the price limit is 3,466 words and costs about 20.4 million gas, which fits a big block only. A walk across the whole range at spacing 1 is about 6,932 words and about 40.7 million gas, more than a big block holds, so it must be split into at least two transactions with intermediate price limits. At spacing 10 the walk from tick 0 is 347 words and about 2.08 million gas, which fits a small block when the transaction does little else. The deployed routers make the long walk the default: Universal Router 2.1.2 passed MIN_SQRT_PRICE + 1 or MAX_SQRT_PRICE - 1 in 5 of 5 traced swaps and seven other swap callers did the same in 29 traced swaps. A swap sent through them that uses up the liquidity on its side walks every remaining word (src/libraries/SwapMath.sol:63-75) and runs out of gas in a small block at spacing 1. The three levers of F-039 stay as described there: dust positions on every tick (src/PoolManager.sol:145-184), a swap past the last position, and a pool id initialized at an extreme price by a third party (src/PoolManager.sol:117-142). The measurements were taken on the contract deployed at 0x12D4Fd9C5DeDd00ab8a0bCe2CF0167bbf94b6B1F. The cycle 3 critic notes that this is other bytecode than a build of this checkout, so the figures describe the chain's price for the storage reads and writes that the loop in src performs and may differ by small amounts for a new build.
findings.impact: No funds leave the PoolManager and no position is frozen. Two mined liquidity removals used 60,628 and 60,415 gas in the modifyLiquidity frame, and Pool.modifyLiquidity has no loop (src/libraries/Pool.sol:146-238). The cost falls on swappers, arbitrageurs and contracts that need one atomic swap in the 9 pools with tick spacing 1 and the 31 pools with spacing 10. A swap that crosses more than about 95 freshly written ticks, or more than about 504 empty words, has to go to a big block or be split.
findings.preconditions: A pool with tick spacing 1 or 10. For the dust position lever the attacker pays the gas of one liquidity addition per tick. The victim sends the swap to a small block through a router that passes the extreme price limit, or the swap sits in a contract that cannot split it.
findings.mitigations: Routers and keepers on HyperEVM should pass a price limit near the expected end price and split long walks. Contracts that depend on one atomic swap should use pools with tick spacing 60 or more, where the walk from tick 0 is 58 words and about 380,000 gas. Pool creators can initialize the pool ids they intend to use at the market price.

cleared.check: Critic gap from cycles 2 and 3: do the special addresses answer the PoolManager differently when it is an inner frame with another transaction origin? Sixteen call shapes (P1 with value 1 wei and with zero value, P2 transfer of 0 and of 1, P3 balanceOf under STATICCALL, the ten IHooks selectors of P5 and unlockCallback of P7) against 45 targets: precompiles 0x05 to 0x0a, read precompiles 0x0800 to 0x0814, the HYPE bridge address, CoreWriter, WHYPE, the CoreDepositWallet, USDC, the AQAv2 treasury address, the USDC system address, the system interest address, three EntryPoints, Multicall3, Permit2, the deterministic deployer, CreateX, the PoolManager owner, PositionManager and the zero address.
cleared.result: No difference. Every shape gave the same success flag and return data from a top level call sent as the PoolManager and from a forwarding stub placed at the PoolManager address by state override and called by another account. 0x0809 answers every shape with the L1 block number, and the direct call and the stub call returned the same number whenever both ran against the same block. Cycle 2 measured that the number is fixed inside one execution, so it gives no credit as a currency (src/PoolManager.sol:358-360) and fails as a token because the answer is not 1 (src/types/Currency.sol:64-74). The other twenty read precompiles fail every shape in both frames. CoreWriter and the CoreDepositWallet revert on every shape. The bridge address accepts only empty calldata. WHYPE accepts every selector through its fallback and returns no data, so a hook call to it fails the length test (src/libraries/Hooks.sol:152-154). This closes lead L-209 for HyperEVM.
cleared.source: https://rpc.hyperliquid.xyz/evm eth_call with state override in batches, also https://rpc.hypurrscan.io and https://hyperliquid-json-rpc.stakely.io; https://1rpc.io/hyperliquid for the bridge address, CoreWriter, WHYPE, the CoreDepositWallet and USDC; queried 2026-11-23

cleared.check: Lead L-179: can the public Overseer functions mint and burnAndRedeemIfPossible trigger stHYPE.syncSupply and so move the stHYPE rate?
cleared.result: No, by measurement on the official node. Inside one eth_call, with Multicall3 code placed at a real holder's address by state override, I read balancePerShare, totalSupply, totalSupplyRaw, syncStart, syncEnd and rewardsToSync on stHYPE before and after each Overseer call. mint with 1 HYPE raised the supply by exactly 1 token and burnAndRedeemIfPossible of 0.1 stHYPE lowered it by exactly 0.1. balancePerShare, syncStart (1795375980), syncEnd and rewardsToSync were unchanged. syncSupply always writes syncStart (stHYPE.sol lines 392 to 414), so neither call reached it. redeem(0) reverted for this caller, so a successful redeem was not exercised. The Overseer implementation contains the syncSupply selector 0xc693965d, as its rebase function must.

cleared.check: Lead L-240: does a HYPE system transaction create HYPE on the EVM side, or is the value taken from the bridge address?
cleared.result: It is taken from the bridge address. For four blocks with exactly one HYPE system transfer and no other transaction touching either account, the balance of 0x2222222222222222222222222222222222222222 fell by exactly the value and the recipient's balance rose by it, on two archive endpoints. The transfers carry 30,000 gas and empty calldata. A simulated call of that shape to the PoolManager reverts, because the PoolManager has no receive function, so such a transfer cannot raise its balance. All 46 observed HYPE system transfers went to accounts without code, so I did not see what HyperCore does when the recipient reverts.
cleared.source: https://rpc.purroofgroup.com and https://hyperliquid.drpc.org eth_getBalance at blocks 51,993,002 to 51,993,201; https://rpc.purroofgroup.com debug_traceCall from 0x2222222222222222222222222222222222222222 to the PoolManager with 30,000 gas

cleared.check: Which system transactions can an ordinary HyperCore account cause, which need a validator vote, and can any of them reach the PoolManager or carry it as sender (assumptions A2 and A8, the question the cycle 2 critic left with F-020 and F-044)?
cleared.result: An ordinary account can cause three kinds: a HYPE credit from the bridge address to an EVM account, a transfer call on a linked contract from that token's system address, and a coreReceiveWithData call on a linked contract. The targets are the recipient account or the token's linked contract and the sender is a system address. The PoolManager is no linked contract and cannot become one without its owner, and a plain HYPE credit to it reverts. The fourth kind, transfers sent in the name of the AQAv2 linked contract and treasury address, follows user flows in size and names only the two addresses fixed at activation, which needs a validator vote. In 1,927 system transactions none targeted the PoolManager, none had it as sender and none came from the zero address, which is the protocol fee controller here (src/ProtocolFees.sol:48).

cleared.check: The protocol fee controller is the zero address. If some transaction ever ran with msg.sender zero, could collectProtocolFees pay out pool funds?
cleared.result: No. collectProtocolFees subtracts the amount from protocolFeesAccrued with a checked subtraction before the transfer (src/ProtocolFees.sol:54-56). That counter grows only by the protocol share of swap fees (src/ProtocolFees.sol:66-70, src/PoolManager.sol:238), and no protocol fee can be set while the controller is zero (src/ProtocolFees.sol:35-41). On chain the counter is 0 for native HYPE, WHYPE, USDC and Wrapped USDC. A call with amount zero transfers nothing.
cleared.source: src/ProtocolFees.sol:44-57; https://rpc.hyperliquid.xyz/evm eth_call protocolFeesAccrued(address) and eth_getStorageAt slot 2

cleared.check: Work item 1, exits: can an ordinary account make another user's liquidity removal or claim redemption impossible to include or always revert on HyperEVM through gas caps, storage pricing, mempool rules or the big block flag?
cleared.result: No. Removal has no loop (src/libraries/Pool.sol:146-238) and two mined removals used about 60,500 gas each in the modifyLiquidity frame against a 3,000,000 gas small block. burn and take have no loop either (src/PoolManager.sol:291-297 and 332-336). The mempool rule of 8 pending nonces and the one day pruning apply to the sender's own account. The big block flag is set by a HyperCore action of the account itself. System transactions do not use block gas. Filling small blocks costs base fee that is burned and rises with each full block. What an attacker can make expensive is a swap, which is recorded in the finding that extends F-039. A pool's own hook can still block removal, which is F-004.

cleared.check: Lead L-219: an Elysium account sends a child chain message whose target on HyperEVM is the HYPE bridge address, a token system address or CoreWriter. Is a HyperCore balance credited to the Elysium Bridge contract, can a later message spend it, and can this move the HYPE that backs Elysium?
cleared.result: The credit goes to the Bridge contract's own HyperCore account and any later message can spend it, and neither step reaches the backing. In a simulated executeCall from the allowed outbox the Bridge sent 1 HYPE to the bridge address, which emitted Received with the Bridge as user, and a call to CoreWriter logged an action with the Bridge as user. The Bridge sends only the value of the message it executes, and that value was burned on Elysium when the message was created, so its 297,189 HYPE cannot leave without an equal burn. HYPE routed this way lands in a HyperCore account that every Elysium account can command through CoreWriter, so the sender of such a message can lose it to whoever sends the next message. No Received log and no CoreWriter log names the Bridge since its deployment, and the Bridge has no HyperCore account. Token escrow sits in the gateway 0xd97B30dE0bA0C2eAeE942afce77530e06c5F122c, which a Bridge call cannot command without the counterpart gateway as child chain sender. I did not read the gateway code in this cycle and take that from the standard Arbitrum design.
cleared.source: https://rpc.purroofgroup.com debug_traceCall executeCall(address,uint256,bytes) on 0x503D572157113fAaaD4DbeD2647Bb10b949216B6 with from 0xec6b106dfa14428fe5eec2a4065a7be599f02728; eth_getLogs from block 48,956,737; https://api.hyperliquid.xyz/info preTransferCheck

cleared.check: Can an ordinary account link a HyperCore spot token to the PoolManager, so that HyperCore sends system transactions to it or reads its logs as token movements?
cleared.result: No. HyperCore accepts a link when the finalizer deployed the contract with CREATE at a stated nonce, or is stored in the contract's slot 0, or in the slot keccak256("HyperCore deployer"). The PoolManager was created with CREATE2 by the deterministic deployer, a contract that cannot send actions. Slot 0 holds the owner. The custom slot is zero and no function writes a caller chosen slot: persistent writes go to mappings and pool state (src/ERC6909.sol:25-88, src/ProtocolFees.sol:29-70, src/libraries/Pool.sol). Only the owner contract could finalize a link, which is a governance act. A linked PoolManager would still revert on transfer(address,uint256) and coreReceiveWithData, which it does not implement, and it emits no ERC-20 Transfer log.

cleared.check: Cycle 3 critic question applied to HyperEVM: what can an ordinary account make the PoolManager say to the hooks that serve most pools, given that initialize accepts any pool definition that names the hook (src/PoolManager.sol:117-142)?
cleared.result: Little. The hook 0x6227f0128935079abc6993f1166dc5d716032aec (109 pools) and its siblings 0x50c42fd2b1c73a4416535068b9a3a4c5732aeaec and 0xf201641ea2985f079791c6a28c0d3ebfdebdeaec revert in beforeInitialize with error 0x0f2e5b6c when an ordinary account initializes a pool with unknown currencies, and so do five further hooks with the beforeInitialize flag. EquoHook (0x746301d1924933a5454f30a2828f2b3f63cc80cc and 0x176447020847b5ccea98a46e303808d3de22c0cc, 17 pools, verified) has no initialize flag. Its swap callbacks return at once for a pool id that its factory did not register (EquoHook.sol lines 646 to 648 and 667 to 669) and registerPool is limited to the factory (line 300), so a pool created by a stranger gets no fee logic and touches no stored state. One unverified hook is left as a lead. I tested one unknown currency pair per hook, so a hook that accepts some other pair from a stranger is not excluded.
cleared.source: https://rpc.purroofgroup.com debug_traceCall of PoolManager.initialize from an ordinary account; https://sourcify.dev/server/v2/contract/999/0x746301d1924933a5454f30a2828f2b3f63cc80cc?fields=sources

cleared.check: Work item 2, known weaknesses of the execution client: the replay clients patch the state after 18 early mainnet transactions because the validator node handled SELFDESTRUCT improperly, return a placeholder for BLOCKHASH below block 243,538 and treat read precompile addresses as warm from block 8,197,684. Can an ordinary account use any of these against the PoolManager?
cleared.result: No. The source outside src/test contains no SELFDESTRUCT, BLOCKHASH or precompile call (earlier search of src, repeated on 2026-11-23: the only raw calls are src/types/Currency.sol:48 and 73 and src/libraries/Hooks.sol:134). The patched blocks end at 1,531,366, 44 million blocks before the PoolManager was deployed, and no later patch exists in either client. A hook could have been affected in those early blocks and none existed then.

cleared.check: Work item 2, known weaknesses of read precompiles and CoreWriter: audits of AlphaHYPE, dHEDGE and Ventuals and the Papertrade incident of 2026-10-10 show that read precompiles return HyperCore state fixed when the EVM block is built, that CoreWriter actions land after the block, and that the best bid and offer precompile 0x080e can be moved for one block. Does any of this reach funds in the PoolManager?
cleared.result: Not through core. Core calls no precompile and CoreWriter rejects every call shape the PoolManager can produce. A value fixed for the whole block cannot rise between sync and settle of one transaction (src/PoolManager.sol:279-288 and 349-365). The hazard is for a hook or token that prices or reports balances from a precompile: its numbers lag by one block and its price input can be pushed by a trade on the HyperCore book. That belongs to the author of the hook or token. None of the 307 ERC-20 pool currencies shows a balance change without a Transfer log.

cleared.check: Work item 2, incidents: the reported HyperEVM halt of 2026-04-02, the HyperEVM testnet stall of 2026-11-08, stale eth_call results at one RPC provider on 2026-10-20, the block timestamp mismatch between eth_call and execution reported in April 2026, and the theft of a spot token deployer's signing secret on 2026-11-20. Does any give an ordinary account a hold on PoolManager funds?
cleared.result: No. A halt delays every transaction alike and settlement is atomic inside one transaction (src/PoolManager.sol:104-114). The team stated that the April event was limited to the block explorer. Stale or shifted eth_call results mislead software that quotes off chain and core reads no block field. The token theft was a HyperCore deployer account moving its own supply, which is the issuer class already recorded in F-019. The JSON-RPC page confirms that the official node serves only the latest state.

cleared.check: Assumption A1 once more, given the cycle 2 and 3 critic notes: is there new evidence about transient storage on the validator node, and how far does the archive client's block check reach?
cleared.result: Nothing contradicts the earlier clearance and its limit is now stated more exactly. The archive client executes every transaction, system or signed, through one transact call (executor.rs lines 192 to 213) and compares gas used, receipts root and logs bloom with the header for the signed transactions. Receipts of system transactions are filtered out of that comparison (reth_copy.rs lines 41 to 47). The official replay client asserts equality of all signed receipts and of system receipts when the block data includes them (run.rs lines 217 to 264). A stale synced currency left by one transaction would change the outcome of a later native settle in the same block (src/PoolManager.sol:349-356), and such a difference in a signed transaction would break the replay. Both clients reproduce the chain to its head, which the archive endpoints I used show. The validator node itself remains unread.

cleared.check: Lead L-148, second half: which price limit do the deployed routers pass to swap?
cleared.result: The extreme one. Universal Router 2.1.2 passed 4295128740 or 1461446703485210103287273052203988822378723970341 in 5 of 5 traced swaps, seven other callers did so in 29 traced swaps and the Quoter does so in every quote. One caller passes its own limit. The loop stops at the limit and stores the reached price (src/libraries/Pool.sol:344 and 439), so the limit only decides how far a swap that outruns liquidity keeps walking.
cleared.source: https://rpc.purroofgroup.com debug_traceTransaction and debug_traceCall with callTracer

leads.question: Does HyperCore check an AQAv2 treasury designation against the named address, for example refuse an address with code or one that holds none of the token, and can the treasury deployer change the address after activation without a new validator vote?
leads.why: Chain data now shows that the named address needs to do nothing on chain. If the designation can be changed by the treasury deployer alone, the party that can make HyperCore send transfers from an arbitrary address shrinks from the validator set to one staked account, which would raise F-020.

leads.question: What does the unverified hook 0x53884697047ac27de5fbba4a7801fe7812e44080 (12 pools with fee 3000, 1,853 bytes, beforeSwap flag only) do in beforeSwap when the pool id is one that a stranger initialized with its own currencies?
leads.why: It is the only hook with more than ten pools that accepts pools from anyone and whose source is not public. A hook that keeps state per hook instead of per pool id could let a stranger's pool change what liquidity providers of the other 12 pools experience.

leads.question: What bounds the gasLimit field of sendToEvmWithData? All 60 coreReceiveWithData system transactions seen in 4,725 blocks carry 200,000 gas and target the CoreDepositWallet. A test on the HyperEVM testnet with a linked contract and a larger gasLimit would answer it.
leads.why: F-044 rests on a 200,000 gas bound for code that runs ahead of signed transactions. The documentation lets the sender name a gas limit and states no maximum.

leads.question: What does HyperCore do with the HYPE when the EVM recipient of a HYPE system transfer reverts: is the HyperCore sender refunded, and is the bridge address left unchanged?
leads.why: All 46 observed transfers went to accounts without code. The case matters for contracts that are HyperCore accounts, for example the Elysium Bridge after someone routes HYPE to its HyperCore account, and has no effect on the PoolManager, which always reverts.

leads.question: What exactly did the validator node do wrong in the 18 patched SELFDESTRUCT transactions of blocks 1,467,569 to 1,531,366, and when was it fixed? The explanation is in commit 39047242b6260f7764527a2f5057dd9c3a75aa89 of hyperliquid-dex/hyper-evm-sync, which this session could not open.
leads.why: It is the only recorded case where the closed validator node executed an opcode differently from revm. Knowing the cause shows whether code at a hook address could have survived or vanished against the Cancun rule (assumption A7) and whether the fix was a fork with a block number.

leads.question: Does Overseer.redeem for a matured burn id call stHYPE.syncSupply or change balancePerShare? The call reverted for the caller I used, and the implementation at 0x2b8698dd4b8addf7ddcabc46c6aedafe5a70b11c is not verified.
leads.why: mint and burnAndRedeemIfPossible were measured and do not reach syncSupply. redeem is the last public path of the Overseer. The stakes are low while no pool holds stHYPE or wstHYPE.

leadResults.answer: The archive endpoint https://rpc.purroofgroup.com serves eth_getLogs over 100,000 blocks, which made a full list possible. 344 pools, 308 currencies, 53 hooks since block 45,998,366. For 306 of 307 ERC-20 currencies the PoolManager balance equals its Transfer logs. The exception is a test token without logs. No Transfer log naming the PoolManager comes from a contract outside the list, so no pooled token has a second entry point. stHYPE and wstHYPE are in no pool. Value held is small: 11.38 HYPE, 14.78 WHYPE, 997.75 USDC and test or launch tokens.

Measured on the official node inside one eth_call from a real holder's address: mint and burnAndRedeemIfPossible change the stHYPE supply by exactly the amount minted or burned and leave balancePerShare, syncStart, syncEnd and rewardsToSync unchanged, so neither calls syncSupply. redeem reverted for the test caller and is left as a low lead. The implementation is still unverified. No pool holds stHYPE or wstHYPE.

The treasury address does not have to send an EVM transaction, sign a HyperCore action or hold a HyperCore account. Its first transaction (nonce 0, block 37,597,803) is an unsigned system transaction that moved 2,001 USDC out of it, it held 0 HYPE before, and the info API reports userExists false and userHasSentTx false. The designation is separate from the authorizeAqav2Role action, which carries no address and was sent by the staking account 0x4E5319dEb1072B01439EE674db5C321d11fd96F8. Whether the deployer can change the address after activation is still unknown and is a new lead. F-020 is re-reported with this evidence.

Same fact as L-180: no signature, CoreWriter action or HyperCore account of the named address preceded the system transfers. The node also sends transfers in the name of the CoreDepositWallet, a contract, so a contract address can be the sender of a system transaction. I found no second AQAv2 token, so there is no example of a designation whose treasury address is a contract. The actor stays operator, because activation needs a validator vote and two deployers with 500,000 HYPE staked each.

The documentation gives sendToEvmWithData a gasLimit field and no maximum. On chain all 60 coreReceiveWithData system transactions in 4,725 blocks carry 200,000 gas, target the CoreDepositWallet and sit before the signed transactions, like every other system transaction (1,927 of 1,927). The archive client leaves the gas of system transactions out of the block total (executor.rs lines 225 to 227). I saw no transaction with another gas value, so the bound is not established. A testnet action with a larger gasLimit would settle it.

A simulated executeCall from the Elysium outbox shows that the Bridge sends HYPE to 0x2222222222222222222222222222222222222222 and calls CoreWriter without restriction, and both name the Bridge itself as the HyperCore user. A later message could spend that HyperCore account. The escrowed 297,189 HYPE is not reachable this way, because the Bridge sends only the value of a message and that value was burned on Elysium. No such message has been executed and the Bridge has no HyperCore account. The gateway that holds bridged tokens was not read in this cycle.

Done on two archive endpoints. In four blocks with one HYPE system transfer each, the bridge address lost exactly the transferred value and the recipient gained it, so no HYPE is created on the EVM side. The second half of the lead is open: all 46 observed transfers went to accounts without code, so the node's behaviour for a reverting recipient was not seen. A simulated transfer of this shape to the PoolManager reverts.

Measured with debug_traceCall on the deployed PoolManager: 5,871 gas per empty bitmap word, 39,059 gas fixed for the swap frame, 10,917 to 31,243 gas per tick crossing, about 60,500 gas for a liquidity removal. A small block fits about 504 empty words where F-039 estimated 1,283. Universal Router 2.1.2 and seven other callers pass the extreme price limit and one caller passes its own. Recorded as a finding that extends F-039.
